lectures.title: Process Grouping & Control: Efficient Resource Management with cgroups

cues.en: In this lecture.
We want to have a look at what is a cgroup in Linux.
Please note this is just a rough overview that I can give here.
Cgroups can do way more things, but at least we get a first impression.
So a cgroup or control groups.
They are a feature of the linux kernel.
It's provided by the Linux kernel.
The idea here is that we don't just have processes that are in a hierarchy, but also that they can
be bundled into those cgroups and those cgroups form themselves a hierarchy.
This allows us to more evenly distribute system resources.
So for example, if we see that one cgroup needs a lot of processing power and another one also needs
a lot of that, then we can define how those resources should be scheduled between those two cgroups.
Systemd heavily relies on cgroups to manage processes and they are in this hierarchy.
The advantages here is that a cgroup can spend multiple processes and even contain other cgroups.
So we really have a hierarchy here.
Why is this an advantage?
Let's take a normal web server for example.
A normal web server might have multiple child processes, for example to execute PHP code.
If we would just limit the CPU or memory resources of the web server, all those child processes would
not be caught by that.
So we if we if they are all in a cgroup, we can limit the resources for that cgroup and we can make
sure that the whole web server, including all the PHP processes and including all the other processes,
those PHP programs might start.
All of those are contained and they don't, they can't, they can't use more resources than we want
to because we could limit that.
Or another example, we could have Firefox and Firefox likes to have quite a few sub processes for rendering
and we could just say like hey, this whole cgroup in which Firefox is running should not use more than
100MB of memory.
This will, by the way, also be the example in the next lecture we'll have a look at that.
How you can limit Firefox to just 100MB of memory.
So this is a big advantage that all those sub processes that we start from a process in a cgroup, they
will also automatically be in the same cgroup as the parent.
The cgroups are used for all processes, so all the processes that we have started, they are already
in cgroups because of that.
So we didn't have to deal with that so far.
Why do we need those Cgroups Well, the one thing I had mentioned that before already, the resource
limiting that we can configure a cgroup to not exceed a specific, for example, memory limit or percentage
of our CPU resources.
So that's already really nice.
But another reason would be that we can also measure how much resources, certain systems consume.
So for example, our web server with all the other processes that it has spun up, how much CPU power
does it use or how much memory?
Um, and we would also have the ability because all of those processes are bundled into a cgroup that
we could for example, just freeze all of those processes.
Those cgroups are especially useful if we want our system's resources to be shared.
So for example, when we are running multiple services now in an application sense, not in a system
sense, but when we are trying to run multiple services or containers, if we are using Docker on the
same server and we want to share the resources of our hardware, then those cgroups are especially useful.
But they are already used on our system and we want to have a look at those.

list.

Here we got a cgroup user dot slice, this is one cgroup and in that cgroup we got this cgroup here

And then from that we have yet another C group here for those processes, or we got here another C group,

So you can see how we have those hierarchy, how all those processes are in C groups and those C groups
can be nested here on our system.
And this allows us to more easily see, for example, if for example, the user 1000 would use a lot
